title: Watch a Band Perform the Sound Effects from Pink Floyd’s “Money,” Using  a Money Counter, Torn Sheets of Paper & More
description: When Pink Floyd record­ed “Mon­ey” in 1972, Roger Waters spliced into the open­ing moments the sounds of cash reg­is­ters, tear­ing paper, an
body:
When Pink Floyd record­ed “Mon­ey” in 1972, Roger Waters spliced into the open­ing moments the sounds of cash reg­is­ters, tear­ing paper, and jin­gling coins. Half a cen­tu­ry lat­er, the Ger­man drum­mer Sina Doer­ing and her band per­formed those sounds live, using a bowl of loose change, a toy reg­is­ter, a mon­ey counter, and a sheet of paper torn on the beat. And they did it all live at Abbey Road Stu­dios, the same place where Pink Floyd record­ed Dark Side of the Moon (on which “Mon­ey” appears). Watch it above, and enjoy.

title: How the Bird Sound Effects in Alfred Hitchcock’s The Birds Were Created with a Pioneering Electronic Instrument, the Trautonium
description:
in Film, History, Music, Technology |   	August 10th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Alfred Hitch­cock­’s The Birds was nom­i­nat­ed for an Acad­e­
body:
in Film, History, Music, Technology |   	August 10th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Alfred Hitch­cock­’s The Birds was nom­i­nat­ed for an Acad­e­my Award for Best Spe­cial Effects, though view­ers raised on more recent Hol­ly­wood spec­ta­cles would hard­ly find its mech­a­nized and opti­cal­ly print­ed avian attack­ers con­vinc­ing. Still, the pic­ture as a whole has retained its eerie, omi­nous pow­er over the last six decades, and a decent amount of the cred­it for that goes to an aspect that has­n’t dat­ed at all: its non-musi­cal “score” by the ear­ly elec­tron­ic com­pos­er Oskar Sala. Many of the threat­en­ing bird calls on the sound­track were actu­al­ly played by Sala on a device called the Mix­tur-Trau­to­ni­um, a pre-syn­the­siz­er orches­tral elec­tron­ic instru­ment of which he was­n’t just the undis­put­ed mas­ter, but the only play­er in exis­tence.
After his accep­tance into the Berlin Con­ser­va­to­ry in 1929, Sala came into con­tact with the Trau­to­ni­um, which had recent­ly been invent­ed by one Dr. Friedrich Trautwein. Inspired to more deeply under­stand the prin­ci­ples behind the nascent tech­nol­o­gy of elec­tron­ic music, and to fur­ther it, he went on to study physics at the Uni­ver­si­ty of Berlin in the mid-nine­teen-thir­ties.
This posi­tioned him well to devel­op new mod­els of Trau­to­ni­um, a series that cul­mi­nat­ed in 1948 with the Mix­tur-Trau­to­ni­um, which, unlike Trautwein’s mono­phon­ic orig­i­nal, could sound mul­ti­ple voic­es at once. The instru­ment proved ver­sa­tile, and indeed com­mer­cial: any Ger­man who grew up in the nine­teen-fifties will remem­ber its sounds from tele­vi­sion adver­tise­ments.


	

The chance to work on The Birds, by far Sala’s most wide­ly heard sound­track work, “pre­sent­ed itself when a for­mer class­mate of Sala who worked at Uni­ver­sal Stu­dios in Hol­ly­wood heard that Hitch­cock want­ed syn­thet­i­cal­ly pro­duced bird sounds for his next movie,” says Google Arts & Cul­ture. “Hitch­cock, who delib­er­ate­ly want­ed to avoid cre­at­ing tra­di­tion­al movie music, even flew to Sala’s record­ing stu­dio in Berlin where he was impressed by the sounds made by the Trau­to­ni­um, which ulti­mate­ly pro­duced all the movie’s sound effects.” In col­lab­o­ra­tion with fel­low pio­neer­ing elec­tron­ic com­pos­er Remi Gassmann, Sala pro­duced a ver­i­ta­ble storm of not just avian shrieks and cack­les, but also the harsh swirl of the ele­ments and the creaks and groans of fail­ing man-made infra­struc­ture. Or at least that’s what movie­go­ers may imag­ine hear­ing in a sound­track that often verges on the oth­er­world­ly, even the abstract — and Hitch­cock knew that the imag­i­na­tion is the place from which real fear aris­es.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: 'Remember Me' Highlights Black Americans' Self-Expression in Early Photography
description: In our era of screens and proliferous imagery, it strains the imagination to comprehend a time before photography. Two centuries ago, an inventor
body:
In our era of screens and proliferous imagery, it strains the imagination to comprehend a time before photography. Two centuries ago, an inventor named Nicéphore Niépce took the very first picture of his courtyard in France by fitting a pewter plate into a camera obscura. A few years later, a professional scene painter named Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre conceived of the aptly named daguerreotype, in which the image could be permanently fixed. He and Niépce both sold their technologies to the French government, which then published a how-to guide and facilitated the global spread of the process. In 1939, the first daguerrotypes were created in the U.S.
As they say, the rest is history. Except, we often only see a part of the whole story. Because the technology was expensive, and therefore having your photograph taken (let alone owning the equipment) was costly, the visual record of the 19th century in this medium is heavily skewed toward affluent, white individuals and families who could afford it. Due to the long exposure time required to capture the images, we also don’t see candid shots, as carefully posed scenes were required for clarity and fidelity.
Joseph D. Marsters, “Portrait of Martha Ann ‘Patty’ Atavis and Anna Whitridge” (1848), daguerreotype, image (visible): 3 9/16 x 2 9/16 inches
Photography was invented decades before the Civil War and the end of slavery in the U.S., yet so rarely do we glimpse real faces that “illuminate the complexities of race, freedom, and agency before, during, and after the Civil War,” says the National Gallery of Art, which presents Remember Me: Picturing African Americans in Early Photography later this year. The exhibition brings forward dozens of images taken of and by Black Americans, showcasing a wide variety of lived experiences in one place.
Fashion, family, and social status are on full display in a range of gelatin silver prints, daguerrotypes, tintypes, and ambrotypes, some of which are colorized. Because many of the earliest formats were very fragile, they were often displayed in ornate folding cases. Several of these will be included with their images, plus cabinet cards and portraits by pioneering Black artists like James Van Der Zee, who ran a prominent studio in Harlem in the early 20th century.
The exhibition will highlight around 70 pieces in the museum’s collection that center self-expression and the entrepreneurial spirit of African American individuals. Remember Me is slated to open on November 7 and will continue through March 14 in Washington, D.C. Learn more and plan your visit on the museum’s website.
American, 19th century, “Portrait of a Soldier with a Knife and Gun” (c. 1863), ambrotype with applied color, image (visible): 1 15/16 x 1 7/16 inches
Fred S. Tisdell, “Portrait of a Young Woman” (c. 1910), gelatin silver print (cabinet card), image/sheet: 5 3/8 x3 3/8 inches
Glenalvin Goodridge, “Portrait of a Cat” (c. 1858), ambrotype,  image (visible): 2 13/16 x 2 5/16 inches
American, 19th century, “Portrait of a Woman in a Bonnet with Pink Ribbons” (c. 1860), ambrotype with applied color, image (visible): 2 1/2 x 2 1/16 inches
American, 19th century “Remember Me, Annie” (c. 1860), tintype with applied color, image (visible): 2 9/16 x 2 1/16 inches
Daniel Freeman, “Portrait of a Couple” (c. 1899), gelatin silver print, image/sheet: 3 5/8 x 5 1/8 inches

title: The Native History of NYC's Oysters
description:
Daily Newsletter
                Who needs IMAX? See a real papyrus fragment of Homer’s Odyssey at The Met.
body:
Daily Newsletter
                Who needs IMAX? See a real papyrus fragment of Homer’s Odyssey at The Met.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            The oyster, writes Hrag Vartanian, is "no incidental New Yorker, but perhaps its most symbolic creature." Hyperallergic's co-founder and editor-at-large visits Mohawk artist Alan Michelson’s poetic installation in Governor’s Island, where about a million oyster shells culled from Manhattan restaurants stir reflections on Native land and historical memory. Vartanian muses on the glorious mollusk’s history, from Lenape shell middens to NYC’s menus to the detrimental effects of their disappearance on our ecosystems. In Michelson’s work, Vartanian writes, “the shells become forces of insurgency, counter-experts that quietly refute settler innocence and its alibi that ‘nothing was here’ before extraction.”Still can’t get a ticket for Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey in New York? Welcome to the club. Here’s a cooler plan: Head uptown to The Met to see a rare, 2,300-year-old fragment with lines from Homer’s epic, now on view at the museum. No hot takes about the historical accuracy of Bronze Age armor required. Papyrus > IMAX.—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

	
		
			The Lost Pearls of New York City
		
	
	
		Walking down Pearl Street in Manhattan’s Chinatown, you probably don’t realize that the name marks the original 17th-century East River shoreline of New York City. In fact, the street was named for a Lenape shell midden that was located on its southern section, which is also believed to have been adjacent to a Lenape canoe landing. It was one of many prominent middens that marked the region, and as Mark Kurlansky explains in his bestselling book The Big Oyster: History on the Half Shell (2006), middens are “the most common marker of a pre-European settlement anywhere in the area of the mouth of the Hudson.” These piles of oyster shells, he notes, were sometimes as much as four feet deep, sometimes buried in the ground, sometimes piled high. | Hrag Vartanian
	
	
		Read More
	


                    
                    
                    
                        
                            Swann Auction Galleries is hosting it's 7th LGBTQ+ Art Material Culture & History auction featuring Tom of Finland, Hugh Steers, Lorenza Böttner, Keith Haring, Andy Warhol, and more.The sale will also include works consigned on behalf of the Detroit Queer Biennial and the Leslie Lohman Museum.

title: Admission Fees at the Lucas Museum, David Hockney’s Reluctant Muse, and More: Morning Links for August 10, 2026
description:

	Good Morning!


Major critic slams the bi
body:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

	Good Morning!


Major critic slams the billionaire-funded Lucas Museum of Narrative Art’s entrance fee.
Three public artworks by Banksy have cost UK taxpayers almost £150,000 in cleaning and security fees.
David Hockney’s former lover, the artist Peter Schlesinger, says he no longer wants to be remembered as the late painter’s muse.


	
		The Headlines	

	MAY THE FEES BE WITH YOU. Los Angeles is a city of stark inequality, which makes the arrival of George Lucas‘s billion-dollar Lucas Museum of Narrative Art especially charged, as Jori Finkel writes in the Art Newspaper. The museum promises ambitious programming and free gardens and public spaces, but it will charge $25 admission and offer memberships costing up to $600 a year. Critics have questioned why a billionaire-funded institution needs to solicit additional public support, particularly in low-income South Los Angeles, where free museum admission has become increasingly common. Unlike Crystal Bridges, Glenstone, the Getty, and the Broad, the Lucas Museum has not committed to universal free entry. Its location offers an opportunity to serve local communities, but its pricing risks undermining its claim to be “the people’s” art institution. 

	
		Related Articles
	


	BANKSY’S BILL. Three public artworks by Banksy have cost UK taxpayers almost £150,000 in cleaning, security, and other expenses, with costs expected to rise, the BBC reports. The largest bill, which topped £85,000, relates to his September 2025 mural on London’s Grade II–listed Royal Courts of Justice, including £50,000 for paint removal and £35,300 for overtime and security. Westminster City Council spent almost £60,000 securing and managing a Banksy statue installed near Trafalgar Square, while removing his 2024 piranha mural from a City of London police sentry box cost £2,200. The spending has reignited debate over whether Banksy’s work constitutes vandalism or valuable public art.
	
	
		The Digest	

	Ireland’s museum sector is reportedly plagued by precarious contracts, low pay, unpaid labor, and toxic workplace cultures, driving burnout, excluding talent, and risking the loss of vital institutional knowledge. [ICOM]

	Several UK museums and cultural organizations are reeling after a cybersecurity incident at Beacon, a CRM provider used by more than 1,000 charities. [Museums Association]
	

	BMW has brought together its legendary Art Cars in Munich, including one painted by Andy Warhol. [Robb Report]

	Notre-Dame rose from the ashes, so why has the UK given up on restoring Charles Rennie Mackintosh’s Glasgow School of Art? [Times of London]
	
		The Kicker	

	A RELUCTANT MUSE. Peter Schlesinger, the artist and former lover of David Hockney, spoke to the Times of London about their five-year relationship, which began when Schlesinger was an 18-year-old UCLA student. The relationship became a defining chapter in Hockney’s life and work. Schlesinger appeared in several celebrated paintings, including Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures). Their relationship ended in 1971, when Schlesinger fell in love with Eric Boman, his future husband of 51 years. The split deeply affected Hockney and inspired some of his most significant work. Now in his late 70s and pursuing his own career in ceramics and photography, Schlesinger says he does not want to be remembered merely as Hockney’s muse.

title: Inhotim Founder Bernardo Paz to Open a Namesake Museum, Right Next Door
description: Brazil’s Minas Gerais will soon see another museum thanks to mining magnate Bernardo Paz, the megacollector behind the Inhotim museum and nature com
body:
Brazil’s Minas Gerais will soon see another museum thanks to mining magnate Bernardo Paz, the megacollector behind the Inhotim museum and nature complex. The Museu Bernardo Paz will turn 311 acres of countryside into a new landscape for “art, nature and community.” The first phase will open in September 2027. 

	“Museu Bernardo Paz is taking root and flourishing from a belief in the creative potential of unexpected encounters,” said Paz in press materials. “This is a place to discover new relationships between art and landscapes of different kinds, between artists and audiences that have not yet met one another, and between the community of Brumadinho and visitors from all over the world. All of this is coming together here, and all of it is for the people.”
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	The museum will encompass more than 20 galleries and pavilions, with commissioned outdoor installations and sculptures, all set in a landscape that includes a lush botanical park and a forest. Locals will be able to take advantage of a community center with a library and art studios. One of the pavilions in development will be devoted to music and dancing, “essential elements of Brazilian culture and identity,” according to the organizers.


			
			
			
	
			
					Rendering of the Michael Heizer Gallery.
									PMCKM Architects
	



	The first phase will include pavilions dedicated to the work of Laura Belém, Sandra Gamarra, Sonia Gomes, Michael Heizer, Anna Maria Maiolino, and Pedro Moraleida, as well as major large-scale sculptures and environments by Torkwase Dyson, Frida Orupabo, Giuseppe Penone, and Mario Garcia Torres. Heizer’s pavilion, the first permanent installation in Latin America, is in progress, and will be dedicated to two large-scale 1993 installations, Displaced Replaced Mass #3 and Negative Wall Sculpture #1.

	“At a moment when there is a prevailing global sense of ever-narrowing possibilities—whether in culture, society, the environment, or politics—we hope that Museu Bernardo Paz will be a place that renews the imagination,” said Paulo Miyada, artistic director, in the press release. “In a landscape full of conjunctions that challenge established notions of museum and landscape, intense opportunities emerge for creation, inspiration, and transformation.”
	

	Paz, who has frequently ranked on the ARTnews Top 200 Collectors list, co-founded Inhotim in 2006 with New York art advisor Allan Schwartzman, who is also chief curatorial advisor on the new museum.  Residing on a 700-acre campus, the museum mixed art, some of it new commissions, with nature preserves and imported flora. It features major pieces by a who’s-who of contemporary art, including international figures such as Doug Aitken, Matthew Barney, Chris Burden, Yayoi Kusama and David Lamelas, as well as Brazilian artists including Cildo Meireles, Hélio Oiticica, Lygia Pape, Valeska Soares, and Adriana Varejão.


			
			
			
	
			
					Bernardo Paz’s new museum will open on some 311 acres of land in the Brumadinho region.
									Niin Content / Debora Guimarães
	



	The new museum complex in the Brumadinho region will also feature some 15,000 trees and a million shrubs, cacti, and flowering plants in a design inspired by Paz’s relationship with 20th-century landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx. Striking arrangements of fruit trees and flowering trees are promised for a space that borders the Inhotim Private Natural Heritage Reserve and the Paz Environmental Protection Area. 

	“Bernardo Paz opened up unprecedented possibilities for contemporary art museums when he founded Inhotim 20 years ago,” said Schwartzman. “With that landmark institution now established, he is moving beyond it into new experimental territory. There is a creative abundance at Museu Bernardo Paz—a distinctive and radical sense of discovery—that will be astonishing in both scope and imaginative force.”
	

	In 2017, Paz was sentenced to nine years in jail for money laundering related to Inhotim, but the decision was reversed in 2020.

title: Fossils and Other Exhibits Stolen From German University in Latest Museum Robbery
description: The University of Bonn in Germany announced last week that numerous fossils and other exhibits have been stolen from its Goldfuß Museum. The univers
body:
The University of Bonn in Germany announced last week that numerous fossils and other exhibits have been stolen from its Goldfuß Museum. The university is now appealing to the public for information on items put up for sale or found on display, in order to secure their recovery.

	The university said it is not clear when the items were stolen, but that it occured during renovation work, which began in December 2023 and is ongoing. In a blog post published August 7, the university shared images of the missing items, and asked the public for assistance.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	“Anyone who has spotted one of the items shown, seen them being offered for sale—e.g. online, on fossil shows, trading platforms or in a store—or noticed anything else that might be relevant is asked to contact the Bonn Police without delay,” the blog post reads, directing the public to send tips to Bonn Police’s Criminal Investigation Division. 

	The university “strongly advise[d]” people not to contact the sellers on their own, but to pass along detais. 

	“Besides the damage caused to the museum building and the theoretical market value of individual items, however, the theft also represents a loss of considerable intellectual significance, as every exhibit stolen from the historical collection, which stretches back to the institute’s founder Georg August Goldfuß (1782—1848), can now no longer be used for research or teaching purposes,” the blog post continues. 

	Per a separate FAQ, the university said that the theft was discovered after certain wooden safety enclosures were due to be dismantled. Workers found the cases broken into and the items, detailed in photos, missing.

	The incident is just the latest theft at a major museum in Europe. While last October’s brazen daylight Louvre robbery has captured headlines and public attention, there have numerous robberies since, including an all-night robbery in Italy in late July in which thieves made off with $4.63 million worth of art.
